The debate arises because foreign investors use investor-state dispute settlement mechanisms to challenge legitimate state taxation, as seen in Vodafone and Cairn cases.
The core conflict is the asymmetrical application of fair treatment standards without reciprocal safeguards protecting the sovereign tax base of host nations.
Energy supply and extractive sectors drive one-third of investor-state disputes, while United States entities account for 17.4 percent of such cases.
Over the last decade, 134 tax-related ISDS cases were admitted, with claimants invoking bilateral investment treaties instead of existing tax dispute treaties in 53 percent.
India has consistently maintained at international platforms that sovereign taxation matters should remain strictly outside international investment arbitration.
Alternative frameworks exist, such as Brazil excluding ISDS entirely by relying on state-to-state dispute settlement and joint implementation committees.
India reduced the requirement to exhaust local remedies to three years in its UAE investment pact, down from five years in its 2015 model.
Treaties should provide investor recourse without creating privileged fast-track avenues that discriminate against domestic taxpayers or undermine regulatory autonomy.
sum.text:
Foreign investment inflows are a barometer to gauge economic success. Bilateral investment treaties (BITs) are among the many factors that lure investors to our shores. BITs assure a steady regulatory framework, allaying concerns of unforeseen costs to investors. However, those very assurances often turn into high standards of protection that investors resort to in order to curtail sovereign regulatory powers. The Cairn and Vodafone cases were examples of how transactional specificities allowed investor rights that are agnostic of the intent of investment.
Some argue that the point is about safety. But what happens when standards such as fair and equitable treatment apply asymmetrically, that is, when there is no reciprocal protection of the tax base?
Another article of relevance in these treaties relates to expropriation. Historical experiences — the nationalisation of the oil industry in Mexico in 1938, the expropriation of foreign owned assets by Cuba in 1959 and the post-World War II nationalisation of industries in Europe — make this relevant.
The fears are not unfounded but are these concerns relevant? Energy supply and extractive industry contribute to a third of investor-state disputes, and so the standards are valid. But how far should these standards of protection apply, especially since the remedy for change in ownership of assets is not interchangeable with policy sovereignty?
Ironically, the countries that enforce these standards are often not in conformity with the rule of law. The US accounts for 17.4 per cent of investor-state disputes settlements (ISDS). Nevertheless, developing countries have to extend bilateral investment treaty protection from policy measures like tax.
Not only do the treaties assign foreign investors rights, such as arbitration in tax matters, beyond those available to domestic investors, but these are incompatible with the position India has held at multiple fora that arbitration in tax matters is not permissible.
This exclusion of tax from investment treaties is not peculiar to India, as many countries grapple with forum shopping. points: US President Donald J Trump announced a diesel deal to purchase hundreds of thousands of tonnes of fuel from Russia, alongside a short-lived energy ceasefire.
The move was triggered by rising US domestic inflation, soaring fuel pump prices, and falling poll ratings ahead of the upcoming midterm elections.
The core debate centers on the hypocrisy of US energy purchases from Russia while Washington penalizes other nations for similar actions.
Trump announced the US would buy 300,000 tonnes of Russian diesel immediately, 500,000 tonnes in November, and potentially one million tonnes the next month.
The announced energy ceasefire collapsed within hours as attacks on gas facilities resumed across Ukraine.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy criticized the deal, noting that Russian diesel exports constitute a negligible fraction of global supply.
A bipartisan group of US senators called for a reversal of the diesel deal, drawing ire from both Republicans and Democrats.
Meanwhile, the European Union adopted nearly 1,600 new sanctions listings targeting Russia's military-industrial complex and ballistic missile supply chains.
India views the US diesel deal with incredulity given that Trump previously criticized New Delhi for its purchases of Russian oil.
sum.text: New Delhi: US President Donald J Trump’s diesel deal with Russia and his declaration of a ceasefire last Sunday, which collapsed within hours, highlight the growing limitations of American policy in Eastern Europe. Trump’s announcement that the US would purchase 300,000 tonnes of diesel from Russia immediately, 500,000 tonnes in November and potentially one million tonnes the following month was met with anger in the US, while Europe largely shrugged, continued imposing sanctions on Moscow and pressed ahead with its support for Ukraine. The deal has been met with a degree of incredulity in India, especially as Trump spent the better part of 2025 railing against New Delhi’s purchases of Russian oil. The deal will do little to bring down diesel prices across the US as Trump heads into the midterm elections on 3 November, which could potentially end Republican control of Congress. The diesel deal and its aftermath are ThePrint’s Newsmaker of the Week. Show Full Article Following his announcement of the deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin, Trump took aim at Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, calling for his resignation on 10 October. Zelenskyy and Trump have had a difficult relationship, stemming partly from the American president’s first-term obsession with Hunter Biden’s laptop and investigations into the younger Biden’s links to Burisma, a Ukrainian company. Their differences spilled into a public shouting match in the Oval Office in February 2025. Although US-Ukraine relations hit a rough patch for parts of 2025, Kyiv spent much of 2025 trying to repair ties, including by offering Washington a stake in Ukraine’s critical mineral reserves. AI agents have simply made these vulnerabilities easier to detect and exploit at unprecedented speed and scale.
Organisations must therefore stop treating cybersecurity as a routine compliance exercise. Regular code audits, multi-factor authentication, restricted access privileges and continuous monitoring must become standard practices. The responsibility of AI developers and research laboratories cannot be discounted.
Network-level restrictions and human approval for high-impact actions should be mandatory. India needs clear accountability standards governing the testing, deployment and monitoring of autonomous AI systems. Regulators, technology firms and business houses must cooperate to frame rules that bolster cybersecurity without stifling innovation.
CERT-In’s warning makes it clear that organisations must secure their digital foundations before granting machines greater autonomy.

That is not a small achievement in a country where the informal sector has historically handled the overwhelming majority of discarded electronics, often through unsafe acid leaching and open burning. But recycling, even at its best, is the last and least valuable step in managing a resource. If India's e-waste strategy stops at "collect it and shred it," the country will keep building bigger recycling infrastructure to process an ever-larger stream of waste without ever asking why that stream keeps growing in the first place, or whether most of what enters it needed to become waste at all.

As the Indian Forest Service marks the 60th year of its inception, the spectacular revival of the rhinoceros in Indian jungles is one of the greatest conservation success stories in modern history. Centuries ago, the animal roamed freely across the Indo-Gangetic Plain. Relentless hunting and rapid agricultural expansion left just 20 animals surviving in Assam’s Kaziranga by the early 20th century.
By the mid-2000s, India’s herd stabilised at 2,500. The Indian Rhino Vision 2020 (IRV2020) was launched in 2005 to push up the population to 3,000 across seven protected areas in Assam. Today, the count exceeds 3,200, with Kaziranga alone housing 2,600.
This resurgence has occurred alongside a broader environmental milestone: India significantly expanded its green cover despite a growing human population. To anchor these habitat gains, the Wildlife Institute of India is currently mapping a National Grassland Atlas. This initiative supports India’s 2070 net-zero carbon target, a goal that the rhino naturally champions.
Using its prehensile upper lip to pluck grass cleanly without uprooting it, the rhino mirrors sustainable land management. Protecting them also safeguards dense grasslands, which act as vital carbon sinks. Unlike elephants, rhinos rely on a solitary, reactive, and localised instincts, depending entirely on intense, site-specific territorial attachment.
Consequently, saving the species requires strict, localised “fortress protection” rather than expansive landscape corridors. Effective neutralization of Chinese threat: China’s Western Theater Command looks after the entire borders with India, unlike India where it has multiple Commands and structures to respond with different officers at the top.
Cost-effective in the long run: Theaterization will help in better planning and military response and also bring down costs. The Supreme Court’s observations came while the bench was hearing an application on child sexual exploitation and abuse material (CSEAM) online when it took up the question of whether children should be kept off the internet and social media altogether.

The tests evaluated the separation of the Crew Module (CM) from the Service Module (SM), two major components of Gaganyaan's Orbital Module. The system is designed to separate the crew module from the service module before the spacecraft re-enters Earth's atmosphere.

Before the crew module begins its return journey to Earth, it must separate from the service module through a carefully timed sequence of operations. The process involves multiple separation events, pyrotechnic devices and jettisoning mechanisms.

The UN Secretary-General has called for an end to the “war on nature”. On Monday, governments gathering in Yerevan, Armenia, will have to confront a more practical question: are they doing enough to win the peace and put the world’s biodiversity goals back on track?
COP17, the UN Biodiversity Conference , comes at a critical halfway point in the global effort to halt and reverse biodiversity loss by 2030. Running from 19 to 30 October, the meeting will take stock of progress, identify where countries are falling behind and, crucially, consider how to accelerate action over the next four years.
The big picture: Think of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework as the world’s blueprint for halting and reversing the destruction of nature.
Agreed in 2022, it contains 23 targets for 2030 and four longer-term goals for 2050 . It tackles the main drivers of biodiversity loss, including changes in how land and seas are used, unsustainable exploitation of species, climate change, pollution and invasive species.
Its best known ambition is “30 by 30” : conserving 30 per cent of land and sea by 2030, the deadline for achieving the UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).
But, the framework goes much further, including financing for biodiversity, reforming harmful incentives, encouraging more sustainable production and consumption and addressing businesses’ impacts and dependencies on nature.
There has been movement. Nearly 90 per cent of the 196 parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity have established national biodiversity targets, close to 60 per cent have developed national biodiversity strategies and action plans and more than 70 per cent have submitted national reports.
But, fewer than half of the national targets assessed by parties are on track. Ambition also remains short of the 30-by-30 goal, while major gaps persist in finance, capacity, cooperation and the data needed to track progress.
As Secretary-General António Guterres told leaders in Yerevan on Friday: “Halfway to 2030, Yerevan is our moment of accountability.”

The automatic weather station records 14 environmental parameters, while the two-camera glacier vision unit continuously monitors changes in the lake and its surroundings. It will provide disaster management authorities with crucial data for timely risk assessment and preparedness against potential hazards.

For beneficiaries aged 18 or above, the notification lists documents such as an Election Commission-issued voter identity card, driving license, Indian passport, and ration card, along with other specified identity documents. The revised scheme includes several new strategic components aligned with India’s long-term sporting vision and preparations for the 2036 Olympic bid and the 2030 Commonwealth Games.

NSFs can now receive assistance of up to ₹50 crore to host an international event, depending on its nature and importance, as well as the number of participating countries and athletes. Proposals will be assessed by a designated committee headed by the Secretary (Sports).

To provide specialised, high-standard training, Olympic Training Centres (OTCs) equipped with the latest sports science equipment are planned.
